**AME27 Embedded Systems Design Challenge**

&nbsp;

1. AI use is allowed on this design challenge, but keep in mind we will ask you questions about your design process in the interview. **Overreliance on AI is easy to spot.**&nbsp;  
2. The challenge is intentionally left **very open-ended.** We encourage you to take the time to learn the concepts you may not already know. You are the designer here\!  
3. Also, this challenge is based on a real project we work on. If you find it interesting, you will likely find our work interesting too 🙂

&nbsp;

**Background**

You are designing the fault-handling system for a BMS (Battery Management System). The BMS monitors the entire battery pack, which is made up of 130 battery cells wired in series. For safety, the BMS must monitor each individual cell voltage, as even if a single cell is over its maximum voltage or temperature, it could be catastrophic.

&nbsp;

When the BMS detects a fault, it has the ability to open the SDC (Shutdown Circuit), immediately deenergizing the car. It should also send the reason for the fault over the [CAN (Controller Area Network)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAN_bus) bus to be displayed on the vehicle’s dash and debugging tools. The SDC is normally-open, so do not close the SDC until you know the battery is safe.

&nbsp;

After a fault is thrown, the BMS should latch the fault state, only clearing the fault and reenergizing the car when a FAULTS\_CLEAR frame is received in the CAN bus. An “active” fault is one that is currently present. For example, if a cell voltage is above 4.2V right now, CELL\_OVER\_VOLTAGE is an active fault. A “latched” fault is a fault that was active at some point, but may or may not be still present.&nbsp;

&nbsp;

**Faults**

* CELL\_OVER\_VOLTAGE  
  Thrown when a single cell’s voltage is above 4.2V  
* CELL\_UNDER\_VOLTAGE  
  Thrown when a single cell’s voltage is below 2.5V  
* CELL\_OVER\_TEMPERATURE  
  Thrown when a single cell’s temperature is above 60°C  
* CELL\_DELTA\_EXCEEDED  
  Thrown when the maximum minus minimum cell voltage is above 0.2V  
* PACK\_OVER\_CURRENT  
  Thrown when the current sensor reads above 200A

**CAN Bus Overview**

The CAN bus is an automotive standard, and the primary means of communication between embedded controllers on our car. The bit format of a CAN frame (a single message sent across the CAN bus) is shown below. For this challenge, the only relevant fields are the 11-bit ID field and the 64-bit data field. The ID is used by other controllers on the network to identify the contents of the frame.

![][image2]

In order to prevent ID collisions on the bus, it is common to allocate blocks of CAN IDs to be used for specific purposes on the car. The BMS controller is allocated all CAN ID’s following the format 0BX in hex, where X can be any 4-bit number.&nbsp;

&nbsp;

ISENSE\_DATA

The current sensor is a CAN device, and sends the current data in the following format at 10Hz (empty data bytes are unused). A positive current represents current flowing out of the pack, and a negative current represents current flowing into the pack (charging).

| CAN ID | Data 0 | Data 1 | Data 2 | Data 3 | Data 4 | Data 5 | Data 6 | Data 7 |
| ----- | ----- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0x511 |  |  | Current in mA (signed big-endian int) |  |  |  |  |  |

&nbsp;

DIAGNOSTIC\_HEARTBEAT

This CAN Frame is sent once per second while the diagnostic tool is connected to the car. It can be used to determine if the diagnostic tool is connected to the car. You may use this information however you wish, or not at all\!

| CAN ID | Data 0 | Data 1 | Data 2 | Data 3 | Data 4 | Data 5 | Data 6 | Data 7 |
| ----- | ----- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0x1CD |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

&nbsp;

FAULTS\_CLEAR

This frame is sent by the diagnosis tool (think an OBD2 Code Reader) when latched faults should be cleared. There is no data in this frame, the BMS should clear faults when receiving it (unless the faulting condition is still present).

| CAN ID | Data 0 | Data 1 | Data 2 | Data 3 | Data 4 | Data 5 | Data 6 | Data 7 |
| ----- | ----- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0x1CF |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

**Shutdown Circuit**

The shutdown circuit (SDC) is a single circuit through all the E-stops and safety devices on the car, controlling the battery pack’s isolation relays. By “opening” the SDC, you are directly turning off the high-voltage battery pack. By “closing” the SDC, you are allowing the pack to energize assuming all the other safety devices are also closed. To interface with the SDC, see the included HAL.h file which has an abstraction function for it.

&nbsp;

**Task**

See the template code below. Every Iter loop, you should read cell data, check for faults (see the requirements above), update the SDC state, and send fault data over the CAN bus. You may organize your code and store internal state however you wish. You are also free to make any reasonable assumptions, just be sure to outline them in your submission.

&nbsp;

The format of the CAN frame(s) sent by you is left up to you, be sure to include your chosen format in your design doc. You must send which faults are currently active, and which faults are latched. Keep in mind, there may be multiple faults at any given time. You should be aware of the amount of frames sent on the bus, there is benefit to fitting more data into a single frame to reduce bus traffic.

&nbsp;

Please submit a PDF outlining your design decisions, and with a link to the code (GitHub or Google Drive is fine, just make sure we have access).

&nbsp;

**Bonus Functionality**

You are free to add other functionality you see fit for a BMS. This is not required for the design challenge, but can add to your submission. Here are some potential ideas:

* Send cell data over the CAN bus for viewing on the diagnostic tool.  
* Store and send values associated with the fault. For example, if an over-current fault is thrown, it could be useful to know the peak current that was drawn.  
* Indicate fault states on the status LED.  
* A configuration interface for setting fault thresholds from the diagnostic tool.  
* Anything else you think could be fun or useful. However, it should not impact the safety requirements.

**Provided Code**

&nbsp;

**HAL.h** \- “Hardware Abstraction Layer” wraps the BMS hardware. There is no implementation for these functions, but you are encouraged to implement them however you see necessary to test your code.

| `#ifndef _HAL_H_ #define _HAL_H_  #include <stddef.h> #include <stdint.h> #include <stdbool.h>  #define CAN_LEN 8 // A CAN message has 8 data bytes #define N_CELLS 130  // Reads the voltage data for all the cells in volts void HAL_ReadVoltages(float data[N_CELLS]); // Reads the temperature data for all the cells in deg C void HAL_ReadTemperatures(float data[N_CELLS]); // Sets the state of the Shutdown Circuit void HAL_SetSDC(bool closed); // Sets a status LED to an RGB color (0-255 each) void HAL_SetLED(uint8_t r, uint8_t g, uint8_t b); // Send a CAN message onto the bus void HAL_SendCanMsg(uint16_t id, const uint8_t data[CAN_LEN]); // Read a CAN message from the bus. // The ID is written into *id and the data into the buffer. void HAL_RecvCanMsg(uint16_t* id, uint8_t data[CAN_LEN]); // Gets the time in milliseconds since the controller was powered on. uint32_t HAL_GetMS(void); #endif` |
| :---- |

&nbsp;

**BMS.c** \- You should implement these functions.

| `#include "hal.h"  void Init() {    // This function runs once on startup  }  void Iter() {    // This function runs periodically at ~20Hz  }  void RxCan() {    // Called every time a CAN frame is received on the bus, using an interrupt.    // Keep in mind, this can be called at any point in the execution of your program.    // You may not use any HAL_* functions here except HAL_RecvCanMsg,    // which is how you can pull the message from the bus.    // An example for pulling a CAN frame is shown below.     uint8_t data[CAN_LEN];    uint16_t id;    HAL_RecvCanMsg(&id, data); }` |
| :---- |
